query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solid, five‐element (Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu) high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, the onset and progression of premelting and melting are governed by an interplay between high configurational entropy (which promotes a random solid solution) and localized strain energy/defect density (arising from atomic size mismatch and limited atomic mobility). These defects and local inhomogeneities lower the effective local melting points, causing early-stage, localized premelting—especially at surfaces and grain boundaries—followed by complete melting once sufficient atomic diffusion is achieved.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, five-element HEA nanoparticles synthesized to yield a single-phase solid solution with a high density of intrinsic lattice defects and strained interfaces.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal ramp (heating) across the premelting and melting regime under an in situ observation environment (e.g., TEM heating stage) to monitor onset and progression of melting.
generation.conditions: Nanoparticles with comparable sizes (e.g., <10 nm) heated at controlled rates in an inert atmosphere; baseline comparison with similarly sized binary or single-metal nanoparticles subjected to identical thermal protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Local defect density, strain fields, and heterogeneous surface sites (especially at grain boundaries) that emerge from atomic size mismatch among the constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy stabilizes the overall mixed phase, but limited atomic mobility suppresses complete atomic rearrangement at moderate temperatures. Instead, localized regions with higher defect densities (e.g., near surfaces or interfaces) act as nucleation sites for premelting. These sites experience a local reduction in melting point, initiating a gradual transition that eventually leads to full melting once heat-driven diffusion overcomes the enthalpic barriers.
generation.predicted_outcome: Upon heating, HEA nanoparticles are predicted to exhibit localized melting (premelting) at defect-rich regions (such as surfaces and grain boundaries) at temperatures lower than the bulk melting point. The overall melting transition will be broader compared to less complex (binary or single-metal) nanoparticles, which should show a sharper, more uniform melting behavior.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles composed of one or two metals of similar size and melting characteristics, having lower defect densities and more uniform melting behavior under the same thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply primarily to nanoparticles synthesized as solid, single-phase HEAs via rapid or low-mobility techniques. Its validity may be limited when atomic mobility is significantly enhanced (e.g., in solution-phase syntheses) or when the particle size effects strongly dominate the melting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative temperature differences, extent of localized melting, and the contributions of individual defect types to the premelting process remain uncertain and require detailed in situ characterization to resolve.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ TEM heating experiments on two sets of nanoparticles: (a) five-element Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles and (b) a binary (or single-metal) nanoparticle system of comparable size. Use a controlled heating ramp and capture high-resolution video to monitor the onset and progression of local melting events.
measurements: Spatial mapping of melting onset temperatures across individual particles (e.g., using electron diffraction or image intensity changes).
Quantification of defect density and local strain via high-resolution TEM imaging before heating.
Comparison of melting temperature distribution profiles between HEA and binary nanoparticles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEA nanoparticles do not display distinctly earlier or spatially localized premelting at defect-rich regions compared to the baseline binary nanoparticles, or if their melting transition is not measurably broader and heterogeneous, then the hypothesis—that local defects induced by chemical complexity drive premelting behavior—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. These methods require high reaction temperatures, and rapid cooling to maintain a high-entropy state at room temperature. As a result, the preparation of high-entropy nanoparticles with a single solid solution can be achieved in a non-equilibrium state by suppressing the formation of secondary phases. In 2018, a carbothermal shock method was reported by Yao et al. to alloy up to eight elements into HEA NPs with the designated composition and size. This method involves a 55-ms heating of mixed metal precursors on carbon supports at a peak temperature of 2000 K in argon and cooling at a cooling rate of ∼105 K/s. The high temperature ensures uniform mixtures of multiple elements by fission/fusion and catalytically driven particle dispersion mechanisms. This work has made an important step in the rapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles. However, this method can only be applied to conductive, surface-oxidized carbon support materials. Since then, more work has been reported on the rapid synthesis of HEA NPs within milliseconds to seconds, including fast-moving bed heating, electrical sparkling, Joule heating and microwave heating.
